method.scope: Sections 1 through Conclusion from sections.tex and its recursive inputs; no headings, tables, figures/captions, references or appendices. Main captions flagged separately.
method.macros: Expand zero-argument newcommand/renewcommand definitions from generated/*facts.tex. Expanded values retain invocation source location and macro name.
method.sentences: Split on full stops only (not semicolons, colons, question marks or paragraph breaks); protect decimal points, leading-decimal fractions, listed standard abbreviations and initial sequences. A nonempty final fragment counts as a sentence.
method.words: English alphabetic words, contractions, numeric literals and alphanumeric hyphen compounds; an internal ASCII/nonbreaking hyphen keeps a compound as one word. Math command names and symbols do not count; readable inline letters/numbers count. Displayed formulas omitted from writing statistics.
method.term_matching: Case-insensitive whole words/phrases. establish and qualify include common inflections; audit/readback/archive/receipt/analogue include common inflections. Codes match whole alphanumeric tokens, including textual occurrences in captions.
method.number_inventory: Values expanded before inventory. Categories distinguish abstract, main_body, main_body_math, main_captions, main_table_data, main_table_notes and appendix equivalents. Citations, labels, refs, URL targets, headings and layout widths are removed. Scientific-notation TeX is recorded as its literal numeric components, and the surrounding expression remains in context/fingerprints. Numbers inside model codes are excluded by alphanumeric boundaries. Literal numbered Section/Table/Figure/Equation/Step references are excluded separately; 24-step prediction horizons remain substantive numbers.
method.numeric_comparison: Each surviving AFTER empirical number must find an identical normalized value and percent/nonpercent unit in the BEFORE evidence pool, with source context retained. Removed occurrences are expected after condensation. Repeated existing values are allowed but flagged when an AFTER count exceeds BEFORE; counts alone cannot prove claim equivalence. A change in rounding requires an explicit documented exception, never automatic acceptance.
method.immutability: Table numeric sequences and inline-math sequences must match exactly in order. All body display formulas are whitespace/label-normalized and compared as a multiset; editorial relocation is allowed. Raw source/figure hashes are also reported for independent provenance.

sentences_detail.text: Dealer inventories connect customer order imbalances to risk limits and balance-sheet capacity.
Inventory affects optimal dealer pricing and observed position adjustment ; dealer capacity also matters for Treasury intermediation .
A position can become large during a holding interval and then return toward its starting value.
Monitoring its largest recorded magnitude therefore asks a different question from predicting the endpoint.
We ask when conditional quantile methods forecast a sampled absolute position peak better than simple historical rules.
An upper quantile of this peak supplies a report against which future recorded positions can be compared.
The comparison uses an hourly client-flow net-position record from one FX market maker and a weekly Treasury-bill net-position aggregate.
Historical headroom and translated-path rules compete with ridge quantile regression and nearest-neighbour quantiles.
Matched controls use the same completed response histories and refit schedules, so each comparison holds the target and those two design choices fixed.
The source-specific rankings motivate an exploratory sequence that separates update schedules, history lengths, predictor sets and penalty menus; the original comparisons remain the reference points.
Three empirical findings define the contribution.

On the two-sided absolute holding-period peak, history- and update-matched regression lowers six-step FX loss by 14.8% but raises Treasury loss by 50.8% (Tables — ); this extends the endpoint question of to a common sampled-peak target.
The earlier FX block retains a 16.6% matched reduction but raises loss by 3.2% against the original primary's rolling reference, so that primary's gain direction does not recur (Table ).
Across 12 additional weekly series, expanding the ridge menu reduces median excess loss from 92.6% to 9.2%, yet 34 of 48 cells still lose to historical headroom (Figure ).

Shrinkage mitigates losses, but short-sample weekly validation selection, including a conservative one-SE rule, does not stably protect the historical benchmark: R2's earlier-period worst excess is +181.4% (Section 7).

Score improvement also separates from risk control: the original FX primary lowers loss by 12.7% while breaches rise from 332 to 376; the 1.83% 24-step legacy gain reverses above an underprediction/overprediction weight ratio of 20.6, and both primary Murphy curves cross (Table ; Appendix ).
Inventory-limit comparisons therefore require underprediction amounts, overprediction amounts and breach counts alongside pinball loss.
The comparison is retrospective, and Section describes its information, statistical and decision limits.
The paper proceeds from related work through the target, methods and evaluation to results, robustness and implications.
Inventory research provides the economic motivation for position monitoring.
model dealer quotes under inventory uncertainty, and studies inventory and information in FX trading.
connects Treasury-market functioning to dealer capacity.
Our observed net-position series supplies an input to this motivation, while the forecasting exercise evaluates passive reports.
Financial path extrema and liquidity buffers provide the closest target precedents.
MaxVaR measures the worst intermediate portfolio-value loss .
studies the maximum end-of-day net debit across payment-system participants, and models a one-sided maximum cumulative payment deficit.
forecasts a payment-demand/resource ratio.
Table distinguishes these targets from the absolute peak of a single recorded position series.
Conditional quantile forecasting and its evaluation use mature tools.
Regression quantiles minimize asymmetric absolute loss ; CAViaR models time-varying conditional quantiles .
Volatility-updated historical simulation is an established alternative for financial scenario construction .
already applies conditional methods and lag/calendar predictors to endpoint intervals in the FX source family.
formalizes consistent quantile scores, and represents their comparison through elementary scores.
We use these established ideas for a common peak response.
Relative to these studies, three findings concern a common two-sided absolute sampled peak rather than a signed endpoint, directional payment deficit or portfolio-value loss.

With history lengths and update schedules matched, FX regression lowers loss by 14.8%, whereas Treasury regression raises it by 50.8% (Tables — ); the original FX primary's gain direction does not recur in the earlier block (Table ).

Stronger shrinkage reduces the additional weekly panel's median excess from 92.6% to 9.2%, but 34 of 48 cells still lose (Figure ); short-sample one-SE selection still reaches +181.4% excess loss (Section 7).

Finally, the original FX primary's 12.7% score gain accompanies 376 versus 332 breaches, the 1.83% 24-step legacy gain reverses above weight ratio 20.6, and both primary Murphy curves cross (Table ; Appendix ).
These are empirical applications of established forecasting and scoring ideas, with error amounts and breach counts qualifying the inventory-monitoring interpretation.
The FX record contains hourly client-flow net positions for one market maker across five liquid currency pairs, as described by .
We use the hourly member of the Net Position Time Series Dataset, version two .
It contains 18,576 observations.
Adjacent observations are usually an hour apart, with weekend-sized gaps retained in their recorded order.
The signed scalar is denominated in source-reported USD.
It belongs to the source family of ; exact equality with their input file remains unverified.
The Treasury input is New York Fed Primary Dealer Statistics series PDPOSGS-B, the aggregate Treasury-bill long position less the short position .
The weekly Wednesday-close series contains 706 observations, denominated in USD millions.

FR 2004A instructions describe market/fair-value positions on a trade-date basis, including eligible forward and when-issued outright positions, with specified settlement-date treatment for buybacks .
Table gives the chronological splits in calendar dates.
The target includes the known issue position.

For example, two future magnitudes can each take values zero or one with equal probability.
Perfect positive dependence gives maximum one with probability one half; perfect negative dependence gives maximum one with probability one.
The identical marginal distributions thus permit different peak distributions.

We call these pre-specified main comparisons the primaries: FX regression at the long history versus the original rolling short-history F , and Treasury regression versus its own long-history frozen F .
Their horizons are both six records.
The longer-horizon FX comparison against the original rolling S is a legacy-reference sensitivity.

Together with the selection and inspection history, this makes the p-values exploratory evidence rather than confirmatory control for the entire research process.

The retained target windows share no recorded observations.
Training histories and wider serial dependence can still overlap.
We report full-grid Kupiec proportion-of-failures tests , plus Christoffersen independence and conditional-coverage likelihood ratios conditional on the first retained hit .
The latter uses the subsequent hits consistently in both its null and alternative likelihoods.
Treasury's two grids contain only 40 and 12 observations, so asymptotic reference p-values have limited precision and power.
The exact nominal-exceedance null also differs from an upper-bound null when the peak distribution has an atom at its known floor.
Long-history regression improves the six-step FX score.
Its primary reduction is 12.7% against rolling F , with a HAC statistic of approximately -5.2 .
Against its own frozen F , the reduction is 14.8%.
The matched statistic is approximately -5.9 .
Table gives the complete original conditional menu and the historical controls.
The long-history gain coexists with more breaches, a distinction developed below.
Short-history regression has a much weaker six-step result.
Its matched score reduction is 2.12%, with an unadjusted p-value of 0.54.
At the longer horizon, the same short-history procedure increases mean loss by 31.5%.
The wider menu still selects =0.01 and leaves that cell's reports unchanged: menu expansion does not repair this adverse case.
Extending history improves the regression comparison, whereas extending frozen F slightly raises its short-horizon loss.
This contrast motivates the ordered specification analysis.
The longer-horizon legacy gain is small and statistically imprecise.
Regression improves mean loss by 1.83% against the original rolling S , with an unadjusted p-value of 0.84.
The six-step primary gain has the same direction in each issue year, while the longer-horizon gain is concentrated in the partial 2017 tail.
The original Treasury regression is less accurate than matched historical headroom.
Its main score increases by 50.8%.
Strict breaches rise from 28 to 54.
Its primary HAC p-value is 0.008 (0.015 with the two-primary Bonferroni sensitivity).
All original Treasury regression and Scaled KNN cells lose to their own frozen F controls.
Each accepted fit passed the numerical conditions, so these losses are forecasting outcomes.
Plain KNN at the short Treasury history reproduces F .
Validation selects the entire eligible pool at both horizons.
Its longer-history, longer-horizon score gain reverses on the twelve-point grid: full-sample improvement becomes sparse-grid deterioration.
Both reports have two strict breaches on that grid.
Coverage diagnostics reinforce the original Treasury regression's adverse breach record.
Table gives the nonoverlapping-grid results beside the FX comparison.
A failure to reject for the historical reference has limited evidential strength in this small grid.
Section shows how expanding the penalty menu changes the original regression result; the comparisons here retain the original procedure.
The exploratory sequence asks which procedural changes accompany the score differences.
We start from rolling F , freeze the update schedule, extend the completed-label history, change to a four-predictor regression, and then change to the original full predictor set.
The parsimonious regression retains current signed position, current magnitude and the two past RMS measures.
Figure displays successive differences in loss units normalized by a common starting reference; its increments therefore sum to the total.
The original sequence combines two changes at its last step.
The four-predictor fit used the extended penalty menu \ .001,.01,.1,1,10\ , while the published full specification used the smaller original menu.
Every Treasury parsimonious cell selected the strongest available penalty.
E3 therefore fits the full specification using the same extended menu and preserves the original splits, refit schedule, tie rule and numerical conditions.
It is a post-result comparison and leaves both published primaries in place.
A wider penalty menu largely removes the original Treasury deterioration.
At the main setting, the full regression's excess loss relative to F falls from 50.8% to 3.43%, and its selected penalty changes from 0.001 to 1 .
Under the common menu, the full predictor procedure has 1.24% higher loss than the parsimonious procedure (HAC p-value 0.685).
The small observed difference does not establish equivalence.
The FX gain persists under the wider menu: every selection and issued report agrees with the original full specification.
At the long history, changing from the parsimonious to the full predictor procedure reduces loss by 10.9% (E3-adjusted HAC p-value <.001 ).
This comparison concerns jointly selected tuning procedures and does not isolate the effect of an individual predictor.
Table retains the update, history, predictor-set and menu steps.
The intercept-only reference helps locate the remaining Treasury differences.
In the displayed Treasury order, I changes loss by -2.0 %, +3.2 %, +6.2 %, +2.4 % relative to F .
The expanded full regression selects the menu's upper endpoint in 3 of 4 Treasury cells.
At the main Treasury setting, expanded QR has 32 strict breaches, compared with 28 for F and 54 for original QR.
Stronger shrinkage therefore narrows the score deterioration without restoring the historical breach count.
An additional panel reuses 12 previously archived New York Fed position series on the same economic-date grid, with all 48 horizon—history cells retained (Figure ).
Expanding the full regression's menu reduces the median excess loss relative to F from +92.6% to +9.2%, but it still loses in 34 cells, compared with 45 originally.
The committed pre-run predictions yield P1: 30/45 against a threshold of 40; P2: 24/48 against a threshold of 36; P3: 33/48 against a threshold of 25.
P1 and P2 are unsupported; P3 is supported.
Shrinkage therefore mitigates rather than eliminates the observed weakness.
The design followed inspection of the original panel results, and the series share a reporting system and overlapping dealer positions; this is an exploratory extension, not independent replication.
AR residual-block replay shows that family choice matters.
At each original refit, OLS estimates an intercept and slope on unique transitions from the union of completed windows.
Ordered residuals are replayed from the current anchor; Appendix gives the exact path identity.
Against matched F and S , AR lowers mean loss in 5/8 and 5/8 cells, respectively.
Breaches rise relative to S in 8/8 cells and relative to F in 5/8.
At the main Treasury setting, AR lowers loss by 20.4% against F and 18.9% against S , with 31 breaches versus 28 for F .
Relative to original QR, AR has lower loss in all 4 Treasury cells; relative to expanded QR33+, it does so in 3/4, including a 23.0% reduction in the main Treasury cell.
This mean-filtered procedure relies on a separate residual-representativeness assumption.
Rank sensitivity changes the finite-sample convention.
The original historical rank is (m+1) ; ordinary empirical quantiles use m , with an interval of minimizers at integral m .
The short Treasury full-pool case has distinct ranks under those rules.
The rank-ablation supplement retains all contrasts, including reversals, and the full-pool KNN identity persists whenever both reports share their rank convention.
Results concern the issued reports under the stated convention.
Loss reweighting distinguishes a robust linear gain from a narrow tradeoff.
For each fixed issued report, write J = U+V , so the original quantile score corresponds to =19 up to a positive factor.
Table shows that the short-horizon FX primary reduces both components.
Its breach count nevertheless increases from 332 to 376.
The longer-horizon legacy gain instead exchanges higher underprediction for lower overprediction, and reverses above a weight ratio of 20.6.
These statements concern constant linear weights on the archived reports.
The elementary-score comparisons in Appendix cross for both primaries, ruling out empirical dominance over the full class of consistent quantile scores.
Horizon diagnostics show that realized peaks and fitted reports have different ordering properties.
Realized peaks increase weakly with horizon on every common issue.
Separately fitted quantile reports can cross; the original long-history Treasury regression crosses on about 29% of issues.
A post-result adjustment that raises a longer report can also worsen its score, as the appendix illustrates.
Table summarizes these checks while the complete archived menus remain available in the supplement.
Conservative selection on an earlier period.

Before the R6 calculations, the archived protocol fixed R2 as the main rule: among the expanded-menu candidates and ordinary empirical I , choose the candidate with greatest shrinkage whose validation loss excess over the empirical best is within one paired-loss Newey—West standard error.
This adapts the parsimonious one-SE preference of ; it is neither their standard CV formula nor a guarantee relative to corrected-rank F .
Each weekly cell has 52 evaluation origins.
R2 selects I in 17/26 cells, yet weekly loss changes have median +5.4% and worst +181.4%, against R0's median +4.2%.
The single T-bill H=24 cell attains the worst statistic; the median also exceeds its fixed 5.0% limit, while 5 cells exceed the 25.0% protection limit.
S1 and S3 therefore fail.
The FX six-step long-window change is -6.3%, versus R0's -16.6%, missing S2's half-gain criterion.
R3 adds purged chronological validation folds and retains 2 failed FX cells in the complete archive.
Original-period R1—R3 results are labelled inspected development results.
All earlier evaluation labels finish before the original validation starts.

A bounded repository audit found no prior evaluation role for these earlier origins; the raw history was familiar, the rules followed earlier inspected results, and this is not prospective or external validation.
Retuning the original three-penalty QR structure on the earlier validation segment also qualifies replication (Table ).
The 2015 FX block contains 1,440 origins, about 12 calendar weeks.
The same QR reports lower loss by 16.6% against matched frozen F 2880 (descriptive HAC p=2.94 × 10 -5 ), but raise it by 3.2% against the original primary's rolling F 720 ( p=0.574 ).
The original gain's direction does not recur; the latter difference is statistically imprecise.
These later, unadjusted two-sided normal readbacks use L=7 under Section 5's bandwidth rule and do not control error across the selection and inspection process.
Treasury bill loss rises by 144.3% in the W=52 analogue, retaining the weekly loss direction on 52 origins.
Insufficient earlier history prevents exact replication of the original W=260 primary; the analogue does not replace it.
No pooled test treats related series as independent.
Keep a historical benchmark.
Historical headroom is a demanding reference for these sampled position peaks.
The weekly results show why a conditional method should be compared with a historical rule on the same completed labels and update schedule before it is used for monitoring.
Default to conservative historical reports in short samples.
R6 shows that adding ordinary intercept-only I to the menu and applying one-SE selection still permits large weekly losses: R2 selects I in 17/26 cells, yet its worst excess over F is +181.4%.

For short samples of this kind, use the historical rule by default and switch to a conditional model only when validation evidence is sufficiently strong; this study establishes no such sufficiency threshold.
Prefer conservative corrected-rank F at short windows: earlier-period I itself loses by as much as +36.5% relative to F .
An intercept-only option and a larger penalty do not establish evaluation protection.
Report error amounts and breach occasions together.
Mean underprediction and overprediction describe the size of opposite forecast errors, whereas strict breaches count their occurrence.
A monitoring report should display all three alongside the stipulated score, since a lower score alone does not establish fewer limit exceedances or lower observed funding cost.
Inspection and inference.
The FX evaluation period had been inspected before the conditional methods were specified, so it is not a clean untouched test.
Later statistical inference and the specification sequence describe that same archive.
HAC regularity, fixed-window predictive-ability premises and the effective sample information behind overlapping labels require care; a nonoverlap grid does not make the observations independent.
Measurement and information timing.
Treasury is a downloaded-vintage replay indexed by economic date, not a reconstruction of historical public releases.
The aggregate can hide offsetting dealer positions and includes valuation and composition effects.
Both sources sample a position process and omit intrarecord excursions; the FX client-flow record is not a complete hedged dealer book.
Coverage and specification.
These procedures have no established conditional-coverage guarantee for these records.
Floor atoms distinguish an exact nominal-exceedance null from the upper-bound implication of a quantile, while Treasury's sparse grids make likelihood-ratio approximations fragile.
Stronger Treasury shrinkage brings scores closer to the intercept-only reference while leaving more breaches than F in each original Treasury cell.
The additional panel retains substantial adverse cells, and the short-history longer-horizon FX failure survives menu expansion.
Matching the menu removes one specification difference without identifying a universal or causal value of extra predictors.
Decision value.
We have no observations of the trading, hedging, collateral or funding decisions needed to measure economic benefit.
A lower stipulated score therefore does not establish lower realized financing cost.
Active inventory-sensitive decisions would also alter the position process that a passive forecast observes.
The empirical object is a measured position magnitude; its connection to a particular inventory policy requires the corresponding decision setting.
Three findings qualify conditional forecasts of two-sided absolute holding-period peaks.
History- and update-matched six-step regression lowers FX loss by 14.8% but raises Treasury loss by 50.8%.

In the earlier 2015 FX block with no prior evaluation role found in the repository audit, QR lowers loss by 16.6% against matched frozen F 2880 but raises it by 3.2% against the original primary's rolling F 720 , whose gain direction does not recur; the Treasury W=52 analogue raises loss by 144.3%.
Expanded ridge menus reduce the 12-series weekly panel's median excess from 92.6% to 9.2%, but 34/48 cells still lose.
Shrinkage mitigates losses, yet short-sample weekly validation selection, including conservative one-SE selection, does not stably protect the historical benchmark.
Finally, the original FX primary's 12.7% score gain accompanies breaches rising from 332 to 376; the 1.83% 24-step legacy gain reverses above weight ratio 20.6, and both primary Murphy curves cross.
Inventory-limit selection therefore requires underprediction amounts, overprediction amounts and breach counts alongside pinball loss.
These retrospective comparisons apply established estimators to a sampled peak.
Prior FX inspection, downloaded-vintage Treasury aggregates, post-result menu expansion and shared panel reporting limit generalization.
They establish neither conditional-coverage guarantees nor benefits from actual inventory or funding decisions.

In the earlier 2015 FX block with no prior evaluation role found in the repository audit, QR lowers loss by 16.6% against matched frozen F 2880 but raises it by 3.2% against the original primary's rolling F 720 , whose gain direction does not recur; the Treasury W=52 analogue raises loss by 144.3%.
Shrinkage mitigates losses, yet short-sample weekly validation selection, including conservative one-SE selection, does not stably protect the historical benchmark.
These retrospective comparisons apply established estimators to a sampled peak.
Prior FX inspection, downloaded-vintage Treasury aggregates, post-result menu expansion and shared panel reporting limit generalization.
They establish neither conditional-coverage guarantees nor benefits from actual inventory or funding decisions.
